The agreement is to be submitted immediately for ratification. I may say that the agreement was reached with the assistance of Mr. Carl
Goldenberg who it will be recalled was appointed mediator some months ago. In view of this development both the brotherhood and the companies concerned have asked that I withhold any action or arbitration on this particular dispute.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: REPORTED WEARING OF NEW UNIFORM ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence did not have an opportunity yesterday to answer a question I asked him. In reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South he said:
-all uniforms are worn under the authority of the minister pursuant to the National Defence Act.
The question I asked related to the appearance of certain members of the armed forces on parliament hill apparently wearing green uniforms. Were those uniforms worn with the consent and approval of the minister, and do they represent the view of the government at this time regarding the nature of the uniform which the united forces will wear?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: REPORTED WEARING OF NEW UNIFORM ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated on a number of occasions, it is the intention of the government, the minister and the department that a number of uniforms will be worn this summer on a trial basis to determine their suitability for the forces in years ahead.
These uniforms are presently in the process of being developed, and they will be issued to selected members of the armed forces very soon to be worn this summer. In this process of development some photographs are being taken in order that they may be shown to members of the armed forces to acquaint them with our plans. It is hoped that as soon as this has been done-and this has been indicated to the armed forces-they can be taken into the confidence of the department at the outset, at which time they may obtain

maintopic: REPORTED WEARING OF NEW UNIFORM ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Will the minister indicate the estimated cost of this propaganda effort?

maintopic: REPORTED WEARING OF NEW UNIFORM ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext: This particular effort will not be costly. The uniforms are being developed in fairly limited quantities for user tests. My hon. friend may or may not be aware that each of the three services was in the process of developing a new uniform of its own. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the opportunity to speak on this bill on clause 2 I, like other members of the committee, reviewed some of the activities of the banking committee and some of the conclusions that we arrived at. I reviewed the minister's answers before the committee, not only in answer to some of my questions but some of those asked by the hon. member for Regina and other prominent members of the committee. The minister enunciated on several occasions that the principle behind the bill was to prevent large blocks of shares being held by individuals and their associates, which in the opinion of the minister, would act to the detriment of banking in general in Canada.
The various amendments to the bill brought forward at that time in my opinion and, I would say, in the opinion of all members of the committee, tended to tighten up many of the loopholes that existed. But there was one in particular that bothered me and it obviously also bothered the chairman of the committee. Since I did not anticipate being here today, the chairman of the committee very kindly followed through for me in his speech on Friday last. I refer to the possibility of individuals and their associates, as defined in the act, at present owning more than 10 per cent of the shares of a bank and adding substantially to their holdings on those occasions when new subscriptions or new share capital may be authorized by the governor in council. As I recall the minister's answers at the time, and I wish I could quote them precisely now, he assured the committee that on those occasions when the Mercantile Bank or any bank would request and obtain permission to increase their authorized share capital, those shares would be disposed of by sale to Canadians only.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The other evening I expressed the opinion that laudable as the minister's intentions
Bank Act
were, and convincing as his assurances sounded before the committee, this intention was not necessarily reflected in ariy of the clauses of the present bill. While I did not question the motive of the minister, I did express grave doubt that the minister or the governor in council would have a legal right to impose this type of condition under the provisions of the Bank Act. I suggested, therefore, that possibly it would be in the best interests of the bill if the minister were to introduce some amendment at the appropriate place that would ensure the pro-Canadian spirit of the act.
Perhaps by way of clarification, before reading the amendment, I should point out the situation as it now exists with respect to Mercantile. Under one of the restrictive clauses, I believe it is 75(2)(g), Mercantile Bank has been given permission to dispose of 75 per cent of its shares over a period of five years if the bank desires to avoid the restrictive features of this particular clause concerning the ratio of liabilities. I point out to the committee that there is nothing in the law that says Mercantile must divest itself of these shares, but the law is quite clear that it must divest itself of 75 per cent of the shares if it wants to avoid the punitive features of this particular clause. Furthermore the committee, at the suggestion of other members, also included a provision to the effect that where a bank is more than 25 per cent owned by non-residents, there can no longer be a transfer of bank shares from one non-resident to another. In other words the whole spirit of the bill has been to retain, as much as possible, Canadian control of our banking institutions.
What bothered me was precisely what the minister had in mind, as I reread the testimony, in those future cases where permission would be granted by the governor in council to Mercantile to increase its authorized shares. What is there in the bill that would prevent such a bank from retaining 25 per cent of its shares in perpetuity simply by buying up 25 per cent of the new issues? This could happen despite the assurances of the minister on half a dozen occasions that this is not the spirit of the act.
I requested the minister to introduce some amendment-this refers to all banks-which would provide that if any individual now owns more than 10 per cent of the shares of a bank and that particular bank does obtain permission to increase its share capital, that particular individual and his associates should

not be able to purchase any of these authorized shares. This in effect would mean that whenever Mercantile or any other bank attempted to increase its size by increasing the authorized share capital, the bank could do so only by the sale of those shares to Canadians until such time as the non-resident ratio was down to 25 per cent, and under no circumstances could those shares be purchased by someone who at that time owned more than 10 per cent of the shares.
This is not a new interpretation. This is what the minister assured the committee on three or four occasions was the intention. I expressed the reservation, however, that although I recognized the sincerity of the minister's desire, I would feel more comfortable if this expressed intention of the minister were transferred into some provision in the bill. Accordingly the chairman of the banking committee, as recorded on page 14152 of Hansard, pointed out that to attain the objective I desired an amendment would be required to another clause as well. Perhaps I should read his remarks so I can interpret precisely what I had in mind:

I think this will meet with everybody's approval.
"I am not talking of a specific bank; I am talking of any bank; and more than one bank is in that particular situation. This would guarantee the carrying out of the minister's intention, as he has stated it on several occasions in the committee."

The chairman of the banking committee went on to say, as recorded on this same page:
The hon. member for Verdun was referring to the standing committee. He is not present at this time, but I might say that if we should reach clause 53, subclause 4 today I would suggest an amendment. Perhaps the simplest thing would be to read it.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will take the hon. member's word that it can be fitted in here somewhere. I have no objection to his amendment but I wonder whether he quite realizes what he is doing. It may be an excellent idea but it does make fish of one shareholder and fowl of another. Suppose that a bank applies for an increase of up to 100 per cent of its authorized capital. Those are the terms which we have discussed for the Mercantile Bank. Is the hon. member for Verdun going to tell those who now hold 10 per cent of the existing capital are they cannot buy any more shares of the new issue and that they are limited to holding only 5 per cent but that a new shareholder coming in can buy 10 per cent of the whole lot? I have no objection to doing that-I have no particular love for bank shareholders-but this is obviously what will happen. This will create two classes of shareholders. The original shareholders will not be allowed to own 10 per cent of the shares. They will only be able to hold 5 per cent, or whatever may be the ratio.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS

I think the hon. member will understand that a shareholder will always be able to own up to 10 per cent of the shares. If the number of shares is doubled, there is nothing to prevent an individual from adding to his portfolio until such time as he owns 10 per cent of the particular banking interest. There are other banks in Canada in the same position. There is at least one bank where one individual owns more than 10 per cent of the shares as permitted under the act. This would apply as much to a particular shareholder as to the Mercantile Bank. So I can assure the hon. member that there is nothing here to prevent an individual in the United States or in Canada-this applies to everybody, regardless of where they live and 23033-9011

what the bank is-from owning up to 10 per cent of the shares.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to put a question either to the "minister" of Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands or to the Minister of Finance on clause 53 with regard to the exact procedure that will be used in a particular situation which may very well arise. Shares of banks are listed and sold on the stock exchange. Owners of shares sell them from day to day. Let us suppose that at a particular time only 24 per cent of the shares of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce are owned by foreigners and 10,000 shares are still available, and at one and the same time several buyers, some from the United States and some from England, buy 5,000 shares through the Montreal, Toronto or New York stock exchange. Only 5,000 shares are allowed to be transferred. Which 5,000 does the minister intend to authorize? Which of the individuals purchasing the shares will have good, valid shares?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this very difficult point was discussed at great length in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs by Mr. Elderkin, who is sitting before me today. I will repeat the answer which he gave at that time. He said it would be a case of first come, first served. The responsibility would rest on the bank.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Nevertheless, as the minister knows very well, these shares could very well have been bought all at the same time and not necessarily transferred or even registered at the stock exchange at the same time. Has the minister given any thought to allowing the shares to be transferred directly over the counter in the office of the bank instead of being listed on the stock exchange? Buyers of the shares would then know whether or not the shares were transferable. An American buyer of shares might say, "I did not know those shares were not transferable". The question is: How will he get his money back from the vendor?
There is one more question I should like to put to the minister before I resume my seat. It is my understanding that options are not considered as ownership. In other words, an American can have an option to purchase 40 per cent of the shares of a Canadian bank from a Canadian resident. I think the minister knows very well that an option to purchase is tantamount to ownership, that it is possible to predict how the person who has the option will vote. How does the minister intend to deal with the question of options?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the answer to the first question posed by the hon. member is that he would get his money back by reselling the shares. The principle underlying the bill as far as ownership is concerned is dependent on registration, and that is within the power of the bank itself. Indeed, the bank is under an obligation not to register shares that exceed the limit set forth in the act. I agree with the hon. member that practical difficulties are involved. However, if it is our intention, as I believe it should be, to maintain Canadian ownership and control of our banking institutions, then this is an inescapable difficulty.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has not answered one question, namely, what would be the difficulty in buying the shares of the bank directly over the counter? Is there any particular difficulty other than that this would deprive the stock exchange of some transfer fees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: We considered this problem at some length when these clauses were being drafted. We believe it would place too great a responsibility on the stock exchanges. The only workable method is to provide that the bank shall be responsible for the registration within the limits fixed in the bill.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Let me put it this way. If it is just a matter of the transfer of shares, let us suppose that an American buys 90 per cent of the shares of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and only 25 per cent are transferred. Would that not mean that the owner of the 25 per cent has absolute control of the bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member knows, he cannot buy 25 per cent. The limitation under the act is 10 per cent for an individual. The test is "registered owner", and that is the only test that can be applied in our judgment. We have examined other alternatives. As I say, if we are to try in this bill, as we should, to maintain a Canadian banking system we shall have to face these difficulties which are very real. In due course people trading in Canadian bank stocks will understand the intention of parliament and will understand the limitations.

I apologize to the hon. member for not having copies of the amendment. Copies are now available and will be distributed. I want to assure the hon. member, and I say this sincerely, that we welcome his thinking on the matter and we want to see if there are flaws in the amendment. The spirit behind my amendment is that anybody who owns more than 10 per cent of the shares of any of our Canadian chartered banks would be prohibited from adding to his holdings. I use the word "his" as applying to the individual and his associates as defined in the bill. It is not intended to apply to shares in the Mercantile Bank more than to shares in any other bank. Let us say a person holds 8 per cent of the shares of the Bank of Montreal. If at some future date the Bank of
Bank Act
Montreal were to decide to increase its share capital and obtained permission to do so, such a person would not be able to increase his holdings beyond 10 per cent of the share capital including, of course, the new shares.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This provision would in no way affect the clause in the bill which states that not more than 25 per cent of the shares of a bank can be owned outside the country. Provided the percentage in aggregate is less than 25, there is nothing to prevent non-residents from acquiring shares. But the amendment would prohibit all persons, whether resident or nonresident, from acquiring further shares if they already owned 10 per cent of the shares of a bank.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: I have no quarrel with the spirit of this amendment or the intention behind it. But in legislation it is the words which are important, not the spirit behind them, and it is for this reason that I should like to have the wording cleared up. I will not press the matter unduly because I do not bother about bank shareholders to any great extent, but I do like to see a little logic in our legislation.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister comment on how this clause affects the establishment of a new bank in Canada, and in particular its effect on the take-over of the Mercantile Bank by the First National City Bank of New York? Last night the minister and I dealt with this subject at some length, and as a result of what the minister said I received the impression that if a person wanted to establish a new bank the bulk of the shares must be owned by men of good financial management capability in order to get the bank off the ground.
In fact the minister said he found no fault with the B.I.F. group owning 53 per cent of the stock of the Bank of Western Canada, and no fault with a bank such as Mercantile being taken over by a United States bank. As a result I must conclude that whenever a new charter is granted it must be done under special privilege. The Bank of Western Canada was granted ten years in which to distribute its stock and the Mercantile Bank was given five years to do likewise. Does the establishment of a new bank require special privilege or a special amendment or special legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are two separate questions involved here. One of them has to do with the establishment of a new bank and the conditions that may be laid down as to the distribution of shares. I do not know whether it will be possible in this country to begin a bank with a sufficient number of shareholders each of whom does not have more than 10 per cent of the shares at the outset. I could conceive theoretically of circumstances in which a sufficient number of original subscribers were found who could get together with sufficient capital to establish a new bank and that, of course, is the ideal. However, I think it more likely that a group of entrepreneurs could be found who could
March 21. 1967

put up the necessary amount of capital and who would be prepared to undertake the original risks of organization, and that they should be encouraged to do so and should be given an opportunity, after the establishment of the bank, of distributing the shares more widely in order to comply with the requirement in the legislation that hereafter no one shall own more than 10 per cent of the shares of a bank.
In the case of the Bank of Western Canada that is what happened. A group of financial people got together, applied for a charter which was granted by this parliament and then applied for a certificate to begin operations. They asked for a reasonable time in order to distribute the shares more widely. Treasury Board felt this was a reasonable request and granted ten years within which the original subscribers should distribute the shares more widely among a larger group, none of whom would own more than 10 per cent.
The Bank of Western Canada, however, which does have a single shareholder with more than 25 per cent, is just as much subject to clause 75(2)(g) of the bill as is the Mercantile Bank. There are two separate questions here. One has to do with the distribution of shares and the second has to do with the restrictions placed on any bank so long as one shareholder owns more than 25 per cent. In other words, the restriction contained in clause 75(2)(g) is not directed against foreigners. It is directed against any bank which has a single or associated group of shareholders owning more than 25 per cent. It is not directed specifically against the Mercantile Bank. It is equally applicable at the present time to the Bank of Western Canada.

With respect to the first question, a bank has to take declarations from the shareholders as to their holdings. The responsibility is laid upon the bank to observe the limitations on share ownership.
With respect to the second question, a bank requires my approval in order to offer to enter into an agreement with another bank. The amalgamation cannot take place without the approval of the government. So I believe there are as many safeguards as possible unless one were to have a complete prohibition, and I doubt the wisdom of that. Short of that, the government has complete control over future amalgamations. It would be impossible for an amalgamation to be effected in any way without the permission and knowledge of the government.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to speak at some length on clause 75(2)(g), but in view of the general agreement on the part of members and the arrangements which have been made to expedite debate I shall restrain my desire to outline in considerable detail the unusual peregrinations of the government in its retreat in connection with the Mercantile Bank. I doubt that in the history of our country there has been the equal of the sinuous course taken by the government in connection with this matter.
Finally, after having been assured in this house only a few weeks ago by the Prime Minister that there would be no retreat from
the stand taken, the government swallowed its words and knuckled down to the demands of United States financiers in the persons of the Rockefellers. Indeed, so successful has Mr. Rockefeller been that he is now advising Canadians on other economic matters. In particular he is suggesting that we should establish between Canada and the United States free trade along the lines of the auto agreement which agreement has revealed already, as I pointed out it would, that Canadians are suffering as a result of the action taken by this government in bringing about the agreement.
Let us review what has happened. I am glad the Minister without Portfolio-the former minister of finance-is here, because he has made a study of this subject unequalled by that of any other member of the house. Indeed, when he was head of a royal commission in the 1950's he dealt at length with the need to preserve in Canada the ownership of banking institutions operating in this nation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Let us go back to July of 1966 when the present Minister of Finance, the anointed saviour of right wing Liberalism, decided to leave the former minister in a most unenviable position. He abandoned the principles that were enunciated by the former minister and he ignored the pious declarations of the Prime Minister and other members of the government that the government of Canada was going to take a strong stand in connection with the Mercantile Bank.
In July the announcement was made that the First National City Bank of New York would be required to divest itself of 75 per cent of its interest in the Mercantile Bank within 18 months, and reverse its ownership by issuing new shares or be subject to having its growth restricted by proposed changes in the Bank Act. The Minister of Finance planned to restrict the ownership of bank stock by an individual to 10 per cent. This provision was to apply also to the Mercantile Bank. The penalty for failure of the First National Bank to comply with the directions of the government of Canada was to be the same as that contained in the proposals of his predecessor in office. The Mercantile Bank's growth would be restricted to 20 times its authorized capital. All through the succeeding months the government stood firm. Fears were expressed that it would not stand firm because, after all, the record throughout the period of office of the present administration has been one of declaration, expounding.

determination and retreat. That has been its course through the years. The Prime Minister said when I faced him with this situation-I could give chapter and verse but I do not want to speak at length on this occasion-that the government would not retreat. First the government went its way and then the Gordon way. Then it went both ways and then it met itself coming back. To continue the analogy, the government got there before it left and returned before it arrived. What a performance this has been. Never before has this nation witnessed a greater conglomeration of insipidity-declarations, determination and retreat.
Let me now read from a book written by the Minister without Portfolio. It states on the cover:
What is Canada's political and economic future?
The author examines the role that Canada should play in shaping her own destiny.
The book in entitled "A Choice for Canada". I know the Minister of Finance has read this book because he told me on one occasion in the course of cross-Are about the beneAt he had derived through reading it. Let us see what is said in this book by the former minister of Anance, that man who has such wide knowledge that he used to take bankrupt corporations and turn them into corporations that were more bankrupt than when he started. That is what he did. I could give a perfect example of that but I do not intend to divert from setting forth fully what I have in mind.
Let me quote from page 94 of this book. This is what was written by the minister:
I said the same sort of thing nearly five years before that in a speech entitled, "Whither Canada 

Satellite or independent nation?" This was severely criticized at the time-
Let me skip a paragraph or two. The following was written:
Amendments to the legislation governing federally incorporated insurance, trust, and loan companies in the fall of 1964 provided for their continued control in Canada. It was announced at the same time that similar amendments would be included in the revision of the Bank Act and made retroactive to the date of the announcement. Just prior to this, the president of the First National City Bank of New York came to Ottawa to inquire 23033-902

When the minister says that I believe him because no matter how one may disagree with some of his ideas the statements of fact he has made in the house have invariably been unchallenged. I can pay no greater tribute to him than to say that is his reputation. In reference to the president of the First National City Bank the minister wrote:
He was advised not to proceed until the coming amendments to the Bank Act were made public. He was warned that, as his bank had no commitment to buy the shares in question, the government would feel quite justified in proposing amendments that would be retroactive in their application. Nevertheless, the First National City Bank of New York proceeded to acquire the shares of the Mercantile Bank, contrary to the wishes of the Canadian government and despite the warning given.

The revision of the Bank Act, announced in May of 1965, provided for the renewal of the charter of the Mercantile Bank of Canada but placed limitations upon its future growth. Immediately, the government was subjected to heavy pressure to remove this limitation.
This incident is mentioned to illustrate how Canadian governments are sometimes regarded by private foreign interests. A strong stand is necessary if the government is to make its decisions stick and if Canada is to retain her independence.

He is in the house, and I know he yearns for the opportunity of placing before the house and the country his knowledge of what took place. This government made its stand; it decided what it was going to do. It reversed Mr. Gordon in part. I refer to the Minister without Portfolio as Mr. Gordon because it is diAicult to refer to "the Minister without Portfolio" and be certain that one is identifying him. What happened? The government made a change, but that change was

going to be final. Then a few weeks ago the government swallowed itself. I wonder why. Where was the heavy pressure against the government? The minister has never given any information in that connection.
Was it pressure from the United States government? Did the American administration decide that it was going to determine the course Canada was going to take? I remember that in 1962, during the election of that year, the Minister without Portfolio and other members of the government were not averse to receiving assistance from the United States. There was assistance in the way of manpower and also the expectation of financial assistance in order to defeat the government I had the honour to lead because we dared to take a stand on nuclear weapons contrary to the wishes of the United States administration.

The Minister without Portfolio will recall the gentleman from Washington who with the approval, indeed with the activation of the administration of the United States came to Canada to show the Liberal party how to win an election because Canada had dared to take a stand that was not acceptable to the American administration.
I would like to hear the Minister without Portfolio tell us the story of the meetings with Mr. Harris at the Eoyal York hotel in Toronto and all the contributions that were made by the Americans to help the Liberal party. I would like to hear about that. Then American assistance for the Liberal party was not only acceptable but warmly welcomed. What happened? We wonder who exerted the pressure to bring about the last change that resulted in the bill that is now before us and in particular the clause to which I am referring and the revised version in the amendment of the hon. member for Cartier. I must say to him that as he produced that amendment he brought a smile of pensive approval to the countenance of the Minister of Finance. This amendment was going to be just a little thing and would help out. It has all the appearances of directed spontaneity. It was a beautiful piece of work-so obvious, so transparent. This amendment would bring about a situation that might command the support of the Minister without Portfolio and others who are associated with him in their particular economic views.

What happened in Washington? I recall in 1962 and 1963 that the trouble with the Diefenbaker administration was, they said, that it could not get along with Washington. The Liberal party embraced the assistance, as direct as possible, received from Washington. In the city of Ottawa the American ambassador had his staff meet with the press of Canada for the purpose of showing them, in connection with nuclear weapons, how politically vulnerable the Canadian government was and the means that should be taken by the press to undermine that government because the United States disliked the stand we had taken. That stand is being followed today. That which was heresy is now accepted internationally.
How wonderful the new heaven and earth were going to be. Revelations never produced an equal of the description. Relations were going to be so nice. I need not tell the committee that when the Prime Minister of Canada went to Washington he was treated with about the same consideration by the president as his two dogs were except that he was not lifted by his ears. Only the other day one of the leading exponents of Liberalism in the press gallery stated that the relations were somewhat strained and that when the Prime Minister went to Washington he was kept sitting around cooling his heels while the president was telephoning for an hour or more. What a strange transition. What a metamorphosis has taken place. Those who had the magic means of bringing about good relations with the United States find themselves in a position where pressure pays off. Only in the last few days a book has been published in the United States. It is referred to in a Canadian Press article by Arch MacKenzie. The article says:
A "Mike Pearson massage file" was set up at the White House alter President Johnson became indignant about the Canadian Prime Minister's 1965 proposal for a North Vietnamese bombing pause-
Then it says:
-the purpose of the file was to "hold friendly communications which had been sent to Ottawa over the president's name without being seen by him."
As I have said, the file is called the "massage file." Apparently they have two methods. They have a massage at one end and a massage at the other end whereby they kick the Canadian government around and get their results. Let us consider this article, because the book is not yet in the library and 1 know

You took a stand, then you turned one somersault. That was not sufficient so you turned a second one. Now you have put the legislation in cold storage for five years. We can always depend on the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Chairman, for an entertaining hour or so and he has certainly not disappointed us on this occasion. He appears, however, to have his facts a little mixed. Perhaps the least I can do is to set the record straight. The hon. gentleman is attempting to create quite a false impression of the course of events. When the present senior Minister without Portfolio was minister of finance he brought before this house a bill to amend the Bank Act. Included in that bill was clause 75 (2) (g) exactly in the form as I introduced it in 1966. That clause was to the effect that any bank with an individual shareholding of more than 25 per cent would not be permitted to have liabilities in excess of 20 times the authorized capital after December 31, 1967. Neither in the bill introduced by my distinguished predecessor in office nor in the bill introduced by me was

March 21, 1967
Bank Act
any change made in any of the other provisions relating to the authorized capital of a bank. In all of those respects, the bills were identical.
The committee on finance, trade and economic affairs recommended two important changes. Here I should like to give credit to the committee once again for the very thorough way in which they examined this bill and for the many very useful improvements, some of which were recommended by me or by Mr. Elderkin on my behalf while others were made by the committee itself. One of the most important changes made by the committee was to strengthen this bill in so far as it related to a bank in the position of Mercantile Bank. This amendment prohibits any bank, subject to the restrictions included in clause 75(2)(g), from selling shares to non-residents. This was a very important amendment. As the bill was introduced in 1965 and 1966, shares could have been sold to non-residents as well as residents.
If this recommendation is accepted, and it is now in the bill as reported by the committee, the Mercantile Bank can only escape from the restriction on the ratio of its liabilities to its authorized capital if 75 per cent of the shares of the bank are acquired by Canadian residents. This is a very important and I believe a very useful improvement in the bill.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I now come to the second main recommendation of the committee, and I refer the house to the evidence of the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs of February 22, 1967, when I appeared to discuss clause 75. At that time I read to the committee two messages from the Mercantile Bank. I will read them into the record so that we can have a ready reference. The first message was from Vancouver, dated February 14 and addressed to me. It reads as follows:
As there appear to have been some conflicting reports about the position of our bank regarding the current revision of the Bank Act, we would like to make the record clear. Being a legally constituted Canadian chartered bank since 1953, we of course have been and are now subject to and governed by Canadian law. Any increase in our authorized capital is subject to the control of appropriate Canadian authorities. At the present time it would be inappropriate to offer shares in the bank to the investing public as some years are needed to build profitability. We would appreciate a period of time to accomplish this work. If the proposed special ratio of liabilities to authorized capital becomes the law, this time is needed. We will give consideration to making shares available to Canadian residents when it is appropriate to do so.

I now read into the record another message I received that day, February 22:
We are pleased to confirm our intent to seek share participation by Canadian residents when it is appropriate to make an attractive offering.
Both of these telegrams were signed by Stewart B. Clifford, general manager of the Mercantile Bank of Canada.
The committee discussed these telegrams at some length, and in order to avoid putting the whole of the discussion on the record, although it is very interesting and sheds a somewhat different light on the situation from that which has been suggested to us by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, I might quote the following excerpts. I was asked the following question by the hon. member for Regina City:
If I may put a supplementary question to the minister, does he consider this to be a reasonable request to meet the situation, so that the committee may have some basis for consideration?
To which I answered:
Yes; I believe it is not an unreasonable request. It is very difficult to have a judgment.
I am so interested in having the Mercantile Bank become a Canadian bank that I hesitate to put any unnecessary road blocks in the way. If the extension of a few years would enable them to market their shares successfully to Canadians, then I say, from a Canadian's point of view, that I think this would be a reasonable thing to do.
The chairman then asked the hon. member for Edmonton West whether he had any further questions to ask. The hon. member for Edmonton West said the following, as recorded at page 3492 of the proceedings:
-I am glad to see the minister's attitude, and that of others, which is to let the Mercantile people get themselves back into reasonable shape, or at least of giving them a chance to get into reasonable shape to dispose of their shares. I think it would be an absolute death sentence for this organization if we insisted on the legislation as it now stands, without a further amendment providing for at least five years and a chance to operate in a very competitive market. This is a fundamental right of Canada that was given in 1871 with the passage of the first Bank Act. Every ten years we review banking in this country and set out the terms, rules and regulations under which banking is to operate.

This is the clause in the bill that the former minister of finance felt was necessary to prevent the Mercantile Bank from growing and dominating the Canadian banking scene. Some of us are a little puzzled about how the Mercantile Bank is to grow into such a monster when we realize that, with its authorized share capital of $10 million, it is about one fifth the size of the next largest bank and considerably smaller than many of the banks such as the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and others which may be 20 times as large.

Because of the philosophy behind the bill that it is our right as Canadians to administer financial affairs in this country we accepted the principle. However, when we considered that the effective date for the coming into force of the legislation would be six months hence, it became apparent that it was not realistic. In six months we would have expected the Mercantile Bank to dispose of three quarters of its shares, 750,000 shares of the stock. We keep proclaiming that we are not anti-American. The important point, having convinced our United States friends that we intend to exercise our right to administer the act according to our principles, is that we should not then adopt an anti-American attitude. If we were to force any United States controlled bank to dump 750,000 shares on the market and dispose of them to Canadians in a period of six months, this would be an anti-American action. I do not care what anyone in the house is inclined to think about it; there is a thin line, but it is there.

Mr. Chairman, clause 88 sets out provisions that are perhaps the most important so far as the agricultural industry is concerned. It lays down the provisions under which banks may make loans to farmers. Before it is passed I should like to comment briefly on one or two points and I have a question or two to pose to the Minister of Finance.
There is no doubt that in this day and age the costs of production of primary products are so high that there is tremendous concern on the part of farmers about the economy of their industry. One of the difficulties which farmers face is that in many instances the manner in which their products are sold causes great concern and grave economic hardship. This is particularly true in regard to certain specialized crops such as fruits and vegetables and products of the dairy industry. These foods are financed and produced by the farmers and delivered to warehouses or storage facilities where they are subject to further processing before they are placed before the buying public.
In the case of dairy products, for example, milk is manufactured into cheese. When this takes place a long period of time often elapses between the time the primary producer delivers his goods and they pass out of his hands until the time he is paid for his product. Very often a tremendous risk is involved because of the perishable nature of the product and varying marketing conditions. There are instances where a farmer may deliver a product such as tomatoes and three or four months pass before he receives payment for his produce. I have used the example of milk products where there may be a lapse of 30 days or more before the farmer receives remuneration. In the case of tobacco and sugar beets, many months pass before the producer is paid for his product.

The question which comes to my mind is, what will be the position of a farmer or a banker in the case of an application for a loan, to which a farmer is entitled under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, for the purchase of various commodities, and what rate of interest will be applied? On the one hand there is the Bank Act which may require a higher rate of interest and on the other hand there is the Farm Improvement Loans Act which permits farmers and all those who fall in the categories set out in the act to obtain a maximum loan of $15,000 at 5 per cent.
I know that if the interest rate is increased to per cent the interest which a farmer will have to pay on a loan may amount to a considerable sum of money and may cause hardship to farmers who are used to paying 5 per cent interest on a $15,000 loan. The difference will amount to $337.50 according to my calculations. Many of these loans are made for a longer period than one year. They may be made for as long as five years or whatever time is permitted depending on the type of loan that the farmer wishes to obtain. However, as soon as he has repaid a certain part of the loan he may want to purchase other

equipment or make necessary improvements on his farm.
I have before me some figures which were provided to me by the Department of Finance. I note, for example, that in 1961 the total value of the loans amounted to approximately $108 million. By 1965 the amount had increased to $202 million, and according to the news release issued by the Department of Finance the latest figures indicate that in 1966 85,553 loans were obtained for a total of $212 million in round figures. It is quite evident that there has been a tremendous increase in the number of loans that have been obtained. The total of loans in the whole of Canada amounts to approximately $394 million. Even with an increase of 1 per cent, an additional $4 million will have to be paid in interest charges. If the additional interest rate were 2 per cent or per cent, it would mean roughly $9 million on the volume of business that is transacted.
This sum does not amount to much when spread over a number of farmers but it does mean that $9 million is taken out of the pockets of farmers to be paid to the banking institutions. This money could be used in many cases to help farmers who have not been very successful. When one realizes that approximately 10,000 farmers leave the industry every year one begins to wonder what the reason for this is. Of course some of those who leave have retired, but on the other hand some of them leave the industry because they cannot make ends meet and they have no possibilities for improvement. This additional cost may prove to be too much for them.
I realize there are many farmers who have obtained the maximum loan permitted under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, $15,000 and then have found that owing to the rising cost of machinery and other essential facilities they require additional funds. And anyway, all those loan companies are financed by chartered banks. Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak to this clause of Bill No. C-222, I think it is fair to make the observation that this is perhaps one of the more important clauses of the bill. It is important not only because of the effect it may have on banking in our country but the effect it may have on the economic activity within our country for a number of years ahead. While it is true that the Bank Act will provide for charters being granted to the banks over a period of ten

years, the effect on the economic life of our country will be more far-reaching than that. The trends and patterns that will be established in the years immediately ahead after this bill comes into operation will, in large measure, decide the future of Canada itself and of individual Canadians as well.
What we in this house must consider tonight is whether or not the wealth that has been accumulated in this country which finds its way into deposits in the banks of our nation will serve the average Canadian or whether that wealth will go to those who can pay the highest amount. This, in my opinion, is one of the reasons our parliamentarians of an earlier era put a ceiling on the interest rate that could be charged by our banking institutions. It is a notable fact, sir, that notwithstanding the many obstacles that our bankers have had to overcome throughout the years, such as depressions, wars and other things, our banks have not been unprofitable. One has only to look at the financial statements of these institutions to ascertain that. This does not mean, sir, that the banks could not have been more profitable in Canada had successive governments come to grips with the problems confronting the people of this nation in relation to finance companies, and the activities in which they have engaged over a period of years.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
speechtext: You mean successive Liberal governments.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Someone says, successive Liberal governments. It is a notable fact that the Liberal party has been in power for the greater part of the last number of years. I recall that for 22 years they had almost unlimited access to power in the nation's parliament. Today we are faced with problems that have grown up during the last few years, problems that are the result of the actions that have been taken by the government as well as actions the government failed to take in coming to grips with the problems that face Canadians in every part of our land.
In this particular clause before us we see embedded the objective toward which this government has dedicated its life, dedicated every effort for a period in excess of two years. I need only point to the rise in interest rates that has taken place in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans, the higher interest rate that was provided for farm syndicate loans, to indicate the attitude members opposite have toward the development of our nation. Indeed, sir, from one end
March 21, 1967

of Canada to the other and in all the four corners of the world, Canada is becoming known as a high cost economy. This is one of the things with which we will have to live and with which successive governments will have to try to come to grips. It is a problem that has been created as a result of the carelessness of this administration.
Now, on this occasion we have a Minister of Finance coming before parliament with predictions. You know, sir, his predictions in the past have had an unhappy knack of raising false hopes in the Canadian people. We need only think of what he said would happen with regard to inflation. We think of what he thought could be the economic situation in this nation. We think of what happened with regard to the housing problem. We think of the increased rate of unemployment which has set in, but I note that the Secretary of State for External Affairs smiles. This is a fact in the city of Toronto and in other places in this country. People have suffered hardship and privation this winter because of a lack of a housing program which was effective. In addition to that, other Canadians have had to pay more for houses they have bought than otherwise might have been the case.
We see a rise in the number of unemployed. We see contractors viewing the future apprehensively, and then we see the Postmaster General laughing. The increase in the number of unemployed in the province of Quebec is just as great as, if not greater than that in the city of Toronto. What I wanted to say before I was diverted by those smiles from ministers opposite was that the Minister of Finance has had a knack of raising false hopes in the hearts of most Canadians. Listening to him and to his colleagues one would almost think that high interest rates were a virtue. We listened to the Minister of Labour the other day as he sought to brag about the effect high interest rates would have on the housing program in this country. Everyone knows-everyone who cares, knows-that the people of this country are reaching a stage where they cannot afford to buy the homes which are necessary to house their families. We have this arrogant government, the ministers of which smile when these things are mentioned, going on their way, bringing before this parliament a bill which is a further successive step in those they have taken to raise the cost of production in this country, and lessened the productivity of the individual members of our society.

It will certainly not be the young, with limited resources, because in the minister's own words they are going to be more of a risk than the well established. They will have to pay a higher rate of interest than those who are well established and on the way to building their futures in our nation.

If this amendment is adopted, our banking institutions will be able to operate in the same way as they have in the past without discriminating against the small income groups and will be able to provide the services which they have been able to provide in the years gone by. This is what I feel Canadians from one end of this country to the other have waited for all too long.
I will not say anything more with regard to the amendment which I moved. All I will say is that if the present bill is passed, the people of this country will band together before too long to organize banks of their own in order to provide the services at reasonable rates of interest.

Mr. Chairman, clause 91 is the most important clause of Bill C-222. There has been much talk about clause 75 (2) (g) concerning the Mercantile Bank, but clause 91 is the real nub of the bill. I recall that back in July, when the Minister of Finance introduced the bill, serious concern was expressed by the members of his party about the formula he presented at that time determining the interest rate. It was a compromise formula to satisfy the differing views in his party concerning the determination of the interest rate. As you remember, Mr. Chairman, the formula was to add If per cent to the preceding average quarterly yield of government of Canada short term bonds, and if the average yield on the government short term bonds fell below 4J per cent, then the interest rates would be freed.
This formula was presented at a time when the interest rates were rising. In the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs the weight of evidence on behalf of the

chartered banks was that the present 6 per cent rate was unrealistic in today's economy and unduly restrictive to the competitive position of the banks. This was the basis of the claim. There was no evidence of any real effect on the profit that the banks enjoyed. Professor Slater indicated the advisability of classifying interest rates into two or three broad categories, namely business loans, mortgage loans and consumer loans, and applying different rates to each class. No action was taken on the recommendation at that time. Professor Neufeld said that the problem would be solved by adding one half of 1 per cent every six months until the interest rate reached 8 per cent. This suggestion also was not acted upon by the government. We in the New Democratic Party felt that a regulatory body should be set up to determine the interest rates and the allocation of moneys to different categories of borrowers. As time went on and more evidence came in we found there was pressure to change the formula that was presented by the Minister of Finance in the first instance. A great deal of the pressure came from the Progressive Conservative members of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I begin by commending your advice to the committee. I believe it would be very helpful to the orderly consideration of this clause if we decided what to do about the amendment that has been proposed which in effect maintains the act in the form it is in today, namely with a ceiling on bank interest rates of 6 per cent.
I would remind the committee that this question was discussed at some length on second reading and in the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. I would also remind the committee that the recommendation that the ceiling should be removed entirely was made originally by the Porter commission, which was appointed by the government that preceded us in office. I shall read just a few words from their principal recommendation. It gives the reason for the removal of the ceiling. These are the words I would draw to the attention of the committee:
-the ceiling stands in the way of flexible lending by the banks in that it frequently prevents them from making loans on which higher rates must be charged to cover administrative costs and risks. Obviously, this is to the banks' disadvantage; more importantly, however, it discriminates against borrowers such as small businesses which, if they are to obtain funds at all, must turn to other lenders which charge rates well above those the banks would ask if free to do so.
That, essentially, is the argument for removing the ceiling. This argument was supported by the Economic Council of Canada in its Second Annual Review, when the council said:
At the same time, the instabilities which have arisen in Canada's financial markets during the past year urge a careful reconsideration of both the needs and possible methods for improving and strengthening Canada's existing framework of financial institutions. More generally, to minimize distortions and instabilities in credit and financial markets and to ensure easier access by homebuilders, consumers and small business to credit, various recommendations of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance deserve careful attention-including measures to promote more competitive credit conditions and removal of the arbitrary 6 per cent interest rate ceiling which currently forces many small borrowers into loans at much higher rates.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support also the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosthern in order to maintain the interest rate at 6 per cent.
I would like to use the answer given by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) himself, to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, on Monday, February 6, 1967. As recorded in the proceedings and evidence of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, volume 43, page 3012, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) the Minister of Finance and Receiver General said:
The process of credit creation is a familiar one. The banks make loans.
Now then, Mr. Chairman, whenever banks make loans, they create credit. According to the very statement of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, what banks lend is money they create. Now if the banks lend money they create, that money does not cost them anything. If a bank creates $100 and that $100 does not cost it anything and if it charges a 6 per cent interest, it makes a net profit of 6 per cent, since that money does not cost it anything. It does not cost the bank anything, since it is money it creates. The Minister of Finance and Receiver General admitted that himself and I will read his answer once more:
The process of credit creation is a familiar one. The banks make loans.
It is credit creation and the banks lend money they create. Therefore, that money does not cost them anything.
Let us see what happens in the case of trust companies, savings banks or caisse populaires. Well, conditions are entirely different. When the caisse populaire wishes to lend money, it must first of all have a deposit. It pays an interest on such a deposit, then it lends it at 6J or 7 per cent interest. And it is only the spread between the two that represents its profit. On the other hand, whenever the chartered bank lends money at 6 per cent, it is
[Mr. Caouette.l
the whole 6 per cent which constitutes its profit, since it is money it creates, as the Minister of Finance and Receiver General admitted himself before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. In fact, he said this:
The process of credit creation is a familiar one. The banks make loans.
Banks grant loans and the minister admits that in granting loans, they create money. Therefore, they lend credit and money which does not exist, and this costs them nothing but they make a 6 per cent profit.
No other organization in Canada or in the world can do the same. The caisse populaire charges 7 per cent interest because it starts by giving 4 per cent to its depositors, while the chartered bank creates money to lend it; it does not pay interest on the money it lends. That makes all the difference in the world. And this is the reason why I find that this idea of allowing banks to increase the interest rate, while allowing them in advance to create the money lent, is an abuse on the part of the Minister of Finance. He is giving to the banks too many privileges.
There is another argument in favour of the 6 per cent interest. At present, under section 91 of the act, the situation has become more complicated. According to section 91, the interest rate is established at If per cent, plus the average of the market-yield on short term bonds of Canada. And that rate is computed quarterly for a period of three months.
That amounts to saying, Mr. Chairman, that every three months, that is on December 31, March 31, June 31 and September 31, after working out their computations, the banks may change and vary the interest rate charged to their customers.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
In that case, the citizen who deals with the banks will never have a chance to know what rate of interest the banks charge unless he inquires once every three months.
This will bring the following disadvantages: just before each new trimester, should the banks find out that the average yield of government bonds has increased substantially during the preceding quarterly period and that this will enable them to raise their interest rate for the next one, they will stop granting loans for the rest of this period and await the next one, where the interest rates will be higher. This means that for some seven, eight or 10 days, banks will arrange the restriction on credit so as to draw a better
March 21, 1967

profit on the credit created at the beginning of the next three-month period.
This will also mean, Mr. Chairman, that the banks will no longer be interested in giving loans for a longer term than three months because, if the market were to improve or if the interest rates were to increase in the following three months, all the money lent before this period would bring in less than money lent after these three months.
And if the banks decide that they had better not make loans for a longer term than three months, in order to benefit from increases in the interest rate every three months, they will then reject a whole category of loans, such as mortgage loans, loans to finance the purchase of furniture, and so on.
Now, we are also told, Mr. Chairman, that when government bonds have reached the 4J per cent level, for a three-month period, restrictions will be removed and banks will then be free to make loans at any rate of interest.
That aspect had not escaped the Minister of Finance when he introduced this bill nine or ten months ago, at a time when rates were very high. Today, banks seem to lower deliberately their rates in an effort to bring back the average yield of short-term government bonds to 4J per cent so that the ceiling on interest rates may be removed.
But on the day-and it might come soon- when the average return on government bonds stands at 4J, per cent, then the limits on the interest rate will be abolished and the banks will be able to make loans at whatever rate they choose, 4, 8, 9 per cent.
That is why I say that various methods should not be used to calculate the interest rate for banks; it should be a fixed rate and 6 per cent seems reasonable in view of present market conditions. That is why we will support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden). I support it not because I agree with the rate of 6 per cent or because I find it reasonable, but because I prefer to see the banks kept to a fixed interest rate rather than allowed to increase or decrease it as clause 91 enables them to do.
Only, I think that even at 6 per cent, it is an unreasonable charge for the banks on the money that they create. It might be a reasonable rate on the money they have on deposit, but not on the money they create, and I think there will be an amendment about it, later, upon which I shall also express my opinion.
In regard to the present amendment, after what I have just said, I think that parliament

This, I think, will be the purpose of the amendment presented by the hon. member for Rosthern, and therefore, I shall second it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on this amendment. I would recommend it to all members of parliament who are interested in retaining a reasonable level of interest at which persons can borrow money. I would also ask those interested in the borrowing of money by the average person to consider several propositions which I shall put forward. It seems to me that with regard to short term borrowing that now takes place under the Bank Act, namely at 6 per cent interest, we have found the government reluctant to make the act effective. In a number of ways we have found that the banks are not lending money at 6 per cent but in most cases at a very much higher rate of interest. It is therefore surprising to me that the committee should agree to allow even short term borrowings from the bank to be subject to an interest rate beyond 6 per cent.
In my opinion it was a fallacy when we enacted legislation to subject overdrafts and the right to borrow from the bank to an interest rate of 6 per cent without a provision for premiums and subsidies being paid on that 6 per cent. It seems to me that we really changed the interest rate without changing the law. I was surprised to go into a bank and to find the bank manager, when I asked if I could borrow money at 6 per cent for a specific purpose, say, "No, that is not the rate we get." I asked him whether it was not true that, the bank rate being set at 6 per cent, he would have to charge only 6 per cent. He said, "No. I will tell you what the rates are for all the banks." He pulled out from his desk a slip of paper and indicated to me what the rate would be at every bank at that particular time. This rate changed from week to week. He could tell me whether there was any advantage in borrowing money from the Bank of Nova Scotia under the small loans legislation, whether it was wise to borrow

March 21. 1967
Bank Act
from the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, or whether I should go across the road to the Royal Bank. I found that in no case were they talking about loans with an interest rate of 6 per cent.
In my opinion the 6 per cent loan legislation has not been in effect for probably a long time. I think it is safe to say that all the banks have found ways of getting around the 6 per cent interest charge, and they will probably continue to do so. For the government to get pushed into the position where it cannot enforce the legislation and has to allow big business to dominate the legislation of this nation, and is not able to amend the legislation to provide a ceiling of 6 per cent on certain types of borrowings from the banks, seems to me to be an odd position for a government to find itself in.
I have listened to this business about the banks being poor. I would suggest that the banks are certainly not poor. I know of one case where I was very concerned about the difficulties in which a finance company might find itself. I found that this finance company, if it ever went bankrupt, would take with it two of the major banks of Canada. The banks are lending money to the finance companies and the finance companies are lending that money at 28 per cent or 29 per cent interest. The banks own the finance companies. Therefore, in effect the banks supply the money to the finance companies and there is no money left at an interest rate of 6 per cent. Why should there be? Why should there be any money at 7 per cent for a farmer who wants to borrow when his collateral is not sufficient to cover the loan? The banks do not want to take any risk, and therefore there will not be any money available to the farmer even at an interest rate of 7J per cent. What bank will lend money on a federally guaranteed bank loan at 5 per cent for farm improvement? The bank manager would be fired if he lent money at 5 per cent when he could obtain an interest rate of 10 per cent on it through one of the finance companies. Any bank manager would be in trouble if he made loans of any size without taking full advantage of the money market.
* (9:30 p.m.)
I think the government should be in a position to come before parliament to enact legislation that would provide money to those who need short term loans with a 6 per cent ceiling of interest. I refer to the chartered banks

of Canada. I believe we should make an exception with respect to mortgage money, because mortgage money has not been available for some time, and will not be available in the future, at an interest rate of 6 per cent. Probably an interest rate ceiling of 8 per cent on first mortgages would provide a reasonable return for loans made in this respect. I think there are many banks and many insurance companies that would get back into the housing field and eliminate the difficulty in which the government finds itself in raising mortgage money for housing. I believe, too, that the interest rate on consumer loans covered by collateral should be limited by the government to 12 per cent. No one imagines that the loans that are made by the finance companies are going to be made at 12 per cent. I believe if the banks were allowed to charge 12 per cent on chattel mortgages they would be able to cut immediately into the small loans business of the finance companies. This would eliminate what no one can doubt is profiteering and gangsterism or stealing of money from people who cannot afford to borrow from other institutions. These finance companies charge 25 per cent interest and all the while hang on to the kitchen sink or the refrigerator in order to see that they get their money.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, when the minister raises the interest rate to 7i per cent he is giving in to the banks. Every time I feel that the banks may be hard up I take a look at the new buildings they are constructing; I take a look at their expansion. I should like to be smart enough to be able to examine the financial structure of the banks and their relationship to other financial institutions, including the hundreds of insurance companies they are financing. I suggest that if one were sufficiently competent to make this examination he would find a close relationship between the directorates of finance companies, banks and probably 50 other companies. These companies in fact control the Liberal government, control this parliament and control the financial institutions of this country. They make it impossible for us to pass legislation that will allow the little guy to go into the financial market and borrow money at a reasonable rate, which will enable him to repay his loan in 20 years without increasing the amount of the original loan by 100 per cent.
If the average worker earning $3,000 or $5,000 buys a home for $25,000 today even at the rate of interest Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation charges, that house does

not cost $25,000 but $60,000 by the time he repays the loan. I suggest it is bad business for any worker to go into debt to that extent. This does not represent 25 per cent of his income; it represents all of his income for the rest of his life. It is my opinion that members of parliament, if they are really representing the majority of the people of this country, if they do not represent the financial institutions and if they do not recall who made financial contributions to their election campaigns, are surely going to provide banking institutions that will allow people to borrow mortgage money at a reasonable rate of interest. This should be done, even if the government itself has to get into the banking field as some members have suggested. I suggest that members who think they are going to bring down the cost of living by sitting in judgment when prices go up, and saying it is the fault of this one or that one, should take a close look at this government's action in increasing the interest rate by 1J per cent.
The provisions of this bill uphold the unfairness, the dishonesty that has been taking place in banking institutions. A businessman may borrow $50,000 but he has to put $10,000 in an account and continue to pay on the $50,000. The bank will use that $10,000, so the borrower really only gets $40,000. The interest rate may be 6 per cent, but if anybody is smart enough to calculate how much interest that borrower really pays, then I feel we should think about that. Surely, in this country we can make a division between the risk borrowing that the banks had to undertake in the past when they went into the mortgage field so deeply. For instance, a few years ago the federal government had entered the mortgage field to such an extent that 40 per cent of the housing constructed in this country was constructed under federal loans. The government got themselves out of that field, but they were not replaced by lenders in the private sector. I am sure that the 7J per cent is not going to provide this type of lending. Surely, we are going to have to take a look at some of the things that will permit us to arrange our financial institutions in such a way that people can make short term loans at 6 per cent, which will mean more than doubling the amount of the loan in 20 years, and at the same time allow these financial institutions to make a profit.
I think we should give consideration to some of the other types of banking in which our banks should indulge, but which are not occurring now. Does the Minister of Finance 23033-904

never look at himself at night in the mirror, when he has returned from a walk downtown where he has seen these trust companies erecting new buildings one after another? Does he never wonder what he is doing which is permitting these companies to construct these buildings? There are so many trust companies downtown that they will give you a piece of silverware if you make a deposit, or they will give you a set of coins. Most of the buildings on Sparks Street today are owned by trust companies that were unheard of 10 or 12 years ago. These buildings have been erected with the money the companies have obtained from people who desired loans. The money that was lent was borrowed from the banks. I am sure that the directors of the trust companies are not unrelated to the directors of the banks. It is not difficult to transfer money from one place to another, and then lend it out at twice what it cost you.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the people of this country are going to be looking at this legislation and wondering what happened to the members of parliament who failed to give any protection to the little person who has to enter the mortgage field. I am sure those people are going to find this legislation wanting in protection for the borrower, under ideal conditions, that is if he really did not need the money badly but was going to substitute it for his assets and repay it at 6 per cent interest. We know this type of borrowing is very limited, but people should be able to borrow under these circumstances when the need arises without having to pay the higher rate of interest which we are setting by the passage of this bill.

The question confronting the Canadian population is, where are we going. We have seen increased taxes, increased interest rates affecting home construction. We have seen this government coming in with a major breakthrough, providing for increased interest rates on farm loans. Even the Farm Credit Corporation has increased its rates over the 6 per cent figure. One can only assume that this government is a high interest government. High interest rates affect the cost of production.
Some years ago, and I speak of 1961, 1962 and 1963, we found ourselves in an advantageous position because of the devaluation of the dollar, which gave us an 8 cent advantage in world trade. The governor of the Bank of Canada in his annual report sounds the warning that if we are not careful we shall cause increases in costs to take place. I do not know the exact page on which he states this, but he says that we must be careful, that we have overloaded our society because costs are increasing more rapidly than in the United States. The United States, it must be remembered, is fighting a war in Viet Nam.
Is there any justification for the Minister of Finance to say that the committee in a genial mood agreed that in the light of everything the interest rate of 7J per cent was justified. Is it justified in the light of government spending, increased interest rates affecting house construction, farm loans, even farm syndicate loans, to say nothing of increasing the sales tax from 11 per cent to 12 per cent for manufactured goods?
I point out that the 12 per cent tax on manufactured goods was applied at the place of origin of the goods. Talking to builders, and contractors all across Canada before the price spreads committee, I learned that the 12 per cent, when multiplied through the various trades, ended up by being 25 per cent. One can only assume that this government is blind to what it is doing to the Canadian public. It is a high interest government, a high cost government blind to inflation.
It is all well and good for the minister to say that the committee reached the agreeable conclusion that the 7J per cent interest rate is justified. It is not justified. The committee's job is to solicit evidence, not to reach conclusions. We, as legislators in this house send various members from each party to a committee; that committee solicits and hears evidence. That evidence must be made available; but any judgment shall be reached through debate in the House of Commons, where everybody-those who have served on the
