speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak for only another few minutes. I intend to make clear to the Canadian taxpayer, the Canadian voter and to the Canadian public generally just how badly the Minister of Finance and his cabinet colleagues are disregarding the facts affecting our economic society.
Here we have an important piece of legislation; we have an amendment which would, in effect, provide for the 1| per cent addition formula. This would affect interest rates from April of 1967 on. We see, looking at the Wood-Gundy Securities Limited report for the week ending March 17, 1967, that the average interest rate yield on government bonds ranged from 4 per cent to 4.7 per cent. Averaging this out, as the minister did on page 14057 of Hansard for last Thursday, we can come to the conclusion that the average short term interest rate today in essence is 4.3 per cent. Taking the 1.75 per cent and adding it to that we arrive at a 6.05 per cent interest rate.
There is absolutely no justification for the 7J per cent rate for the interim period. I listened to the hon. member for Broadview on the amendment he sought to move. His is almost the same amendment I had intended moving. I listened carefully to the minister, and he at no time said that the 7| per cent

rate was too high. He said it was the interim rate, and that once we are working on the flexible formula things will take care of themselves. I can only reach the conclusion that once we work under the flexible formula of If per cent plus the short term bond rate that the rate in Canada will eventually reach 8 per cent.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
If this is so, the minister should serve notice that he recognizes the course he is taking and is prepared to support it. First, this government has increased taxes. Second, it has increased the cost of housing construction. Third, since it came to office it has increased the cost of farm loans as well as interest rates generally to farm syndicates. Fourth, it has increased rates under the National Housing Act. Fifth, it has imposed an 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and manufacturing machinery. The last budget increased this to 12 per cent. Remember, this tax is placed on the original goods, so it amounts to a 25 per cent tax to the consumer, as we were told by an Edmonton contractor who gave evidence before the committee which is studying the question of the cost of living to the Canadian consumer. This man had been responsible for the erection of a huge building. Forty trades worked on it and each added the 12 per cent sales tax to its cost before counting profit. This is the practice in the industry. So the eventual cost of the sales tax to the consumer is 25 per cent.
If the minister continues to stumble along, refusing to accept amendments such as this, I can only conclude that government policy today is one of high interest, high taxes and high costs. I believe this needs to be repeated again and again because the minister seems unaware of what he is doing to the Canadian people. Here we have an amendment which accepts the minister's formula of one and three quarters plus the market yield on short term bonds. In essence this would provide the banks with an adjustable interest rate.
When the interest rate goes above 5 per cent clause 91(9) will come into effect and in essence we will have a 6.75 per cent interest rate. By right today the interest rate would be 6.05 per cent if the amendment were accepted. But the minister says he cannot accept it even though, as recorded at page 3505 of committee proceedings No. 51, he expressed concern about this provision. Since then he has returned to this dogmatic position that high interest rates are necessary. He is not even paying attention to his own words,
March 21, 1967

as recorded at page 14057 of Hansard, that there has been a drop from 5.20 per cent to 4.30 per cent.
The minister has become blind to the effect of high interest rates on our society. The governor of the Bank of Canada has warned us, in his 1986 annual report, about pricing ourselves out of world markets. I urge all hon. members to support this amendment. I urge government backbenchers to protect their own cabinet ministers. If they vote for this amendment they may stay in office a little longer. If this provision stands I hope the Canadian public will say, "Enough, enough. Let us go no further with a high interest rate government".

I do not wish to delay a vote on this amendment. I agree with it, but would like to express my views on it, particularly the first part which aims to retain an interest rate ceiling of 6 per cent.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I have listened attentively today to some of the discussion, particularly in respect of clause 91, and I cannot help but agree with most of the hon. members who spoke. I have made a note of some of the arguments brought forth by the hon. member for Acadia, and particularly by the hon. member for Timiskaming who made some true statements concerning the effect of the interest rate and who also gave a pretty clear picture of the banking situation which prevails across the country at the present time.
I am strongly opposed to the raising of the interest rate. When the Minister of Finance brought in his mini-budget I remember the intention at that time was that it would curb inflation and the rising cost of living in this country. I cannot understand how the minister can turn on the gas with his left hand, and then with his other hand turn another valve. This is the way in which he has been operating. I remember when he brought in his mini-budget the minister was talking about the boom, and that we must slow down but must not break the boom. With one
Bank Act
breath he says one thing and then with another breath he says something else. The minister seems to have this ability, to switch from one side to the other.
I told the minister at that time that when the appropriate measure came before us, if he intended to place restrictions across the board he should not forget to take action to lower the cost of living. We are not stupid; we know that the entire production of Canada is financed through the banks, if not directly at least indirectly. The interest rate is reflected in the cost of production and in the retail price, no matter how we look at it. The minister may attempt to tell me a different story, but he cannot fool me. If he should try to make the people believe a different story, then I do not believe he would be fooling them either. Whenever the interest rate increases, the cost of production increases.
The representatives of the banks say that if they had an interest rate which would be more competitive they could lend more money. This is utter nonsense. Representatives of the banks have appeared before the committee and have spoken to different members. When the officials of the Laurentide Bank appeared they told us their bank would be a bank for the small loan borrower. They said that they wanted to help the smaller borrower. They said that the other banks are not helping these people. At that time I told them that the only reason they appeared before members of parliament to ask for a charter for this Laurentide Bank was that they wanted to obtain more credit for the Laurentide financing operations. That was the reason they appeared before us with the same singsong we hear from every chartered bank.
I do not believe for a moment that by increasing the interest rate to 7J per cent we will be helping anybody in this country. This will place the banks in a better bargaining position among the other financial institutions. We are not by act of parliament at this time permitting the mortgage companies, the trust companies, the finance companies or the insurance companies to increase their rates. What we are doing is allowing the banks to put themselves in a position of saying to these various lending institutions that they can now get 7J per cent on small loans. This will mean they can withhold more money from these other financial institutions. Obviously they would sooner make 100 loans of $1,000 at the higher interest rate than one loan of $100,000 to one of these financial institutions. They are then in a position where they can tell these companies to look elsewhere for their money.

March 21, 1967
Bank Act
I fail to understand why members of parliament do not open their eyes to this situation. They should pay a little more attention to what is happening. The chartered banks at this time are the only financial institutions in Canada permitted to create credit in any real form. Other financial institutions must borrow their money from the chartered banks.
The presently proposed increase in interest rates will not in any way assist those individuals who are forced to make small loans. If anyone is not convinced of the fact, let me refer him to what has happened in respect of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. That corporation began making loans at a rate of interest which varied between 2J per cent and 3 per cent. It is still making a profit because it is still in operation.
I should also like to know why chartered banks do not have to pay a similar initial interest rate on the money they lend. They are creating credit with the use of money for which they are not paying as high an interest rate. Why should the chartered banks be empowered to make loans by using money for Which they pay less? If the banks are poor they should come forward and say they are starving, and require this increase in interest rates in order that they will be able to make loans.
The passage of this measure will put chartered banks in the position of refusing to provide money to these small lending companies. They will indicate to these companies that they also can make small loans at a higher rate of interest than they would receive on the money they could provide to these companies. Perhaps it would be wrong to suggest that this is a form of blackmail, because the banks are being given the authority to do this by an act of parliament. Surely the net result of this increase will be an increase in the cost of living in this country, just as the 11 per cent sales tax on construction materials has caused an increase in the cost of living.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
We have seen interest rates rise all across the country. To now open the back door to all financial institutions to raise their interest rates will cause a general increase in the rate charged by all financial institutions across Canada. What will happen to the cost of living? If you raise the interest rate 1 per cent at the production level, when it comes to the retail level that rate has increased to 5 per cent. If you do that twice, you are increasing the rate to 10 per cent. Will this help the consumers of this country? Will we assist in
(Mr. Langlois (Megantic).]
reducing the rising cost of living if we increase the interest rate on loans from the banks?
This government certainly has a tendency to cause difficulty. The only group this provision will help will be the banks, period. We may say we are entering a more realistic financial situation and our financial institutions will be more competitive with each other; but you cannot separate the directors of the chartered banks from the directors of our finance companies. You find that if you look at the directors of the banks and those of the finance companies, they are sometimes the same guys. If you go to the directors of mortgage companies, you find the same guys. This also applies to some of the major producing companies of Canada. You see the same faces in these fields.
Some figures were given to us in the committee in this respect. We learned that those who were directors of the banks and were also directors of these companies were concerned with a total of about 30 per cent of bank loans. One realizes what a fantastic amount of money this involves when in a friendly, family sort of way the same people are involved in the same interests. I do not have to go too far to illustrate my point. You can go across to the other place and find out how many of our distinguished senators are sitting on the boards of major financial institutions and companies in this country. You can look at those in the House of Commons. There is one cabinet minister who was a director of several companies. I remember that when he was appointed a cabinet minister he was a director of many companies. He was a good businessman, and I have nothing against him for this. But I realize that his companies involved a turnover of $14J billion in one year in production. This is approximately one quarter of the total Canadian production.
He is a very prosperous man. He exercised a great deal of control and had a great deal of say-so in these companies. He had much more say-so in this respect than the small individual who has to borrow from this type of company. Often a bank refuses a small loan to an individual because the work in which he is engaged does not produce enough money and a great many guarantees are involved in giving him a loan. Often the bank manager says to this person, "I do not think we can make this loan; go and see the finance company". The loan at 6 per cent interest is refused by the bank. This person goes to the finance
March 21, 1967

company and borrows the money he needs at an interest rate of 24 per cent, 27 per cent, 28 per cent or 30 per cent. Depending upon whether he has a little difficulty in meeting one or two payments, the interest rate may reach 35 per cent before the loan is paid off. How is it that his name is good when the interest rate involved is 35 per cent, when it was not good when the interest was 6 per cent? I will tell the committee why. It is because the bank was not interested in collecting 6 per cent interest. They knew damned well they would collect 35 per cent the safe way, because these finance companies have the same directors sitting on their boards as the banks. If the minister and his colleagues are not afraid to admit this, I am sure they would see the truth in what I have said.
This is one of the most important pieces of legislation to go through this parliament for years. This legislation has to be revised every 10 years, and now is the time to consider it seriously and not after it has been passed. I agree entirely that the amendment before the house, if it will only curb the rising cost of living that now faces this country, is well worth while. But I do not for a single moment believe that if we were to increase the ceiling of the rate of interest to 74 per cent we would help solve this situation. 1 do not believe that passing this legislation would in any way assist the individual who wishes to borrow a small amount of money. It will just give the chartered banks a better bargaining position with these big financial institutions.
The banks are not suffering. One just has to get out and see where the banks stand with regard to new buildings. I think many of the Canadian people are faced with more serious financial crises than the banks will ever have. If the banks ever reach a period of real hardship, there will be a lot more hollering on the part of the public than we are hearing now. They are in good financial condition at the present time. The banks control the whole system, and they not only control the system but they control the government. We can see this from the legislation the government is bringing before the house.
We saw the Minister of Finance introduce his mini-budget, and he was just about in tears. It was the only time I did not see a smile on his face. He was begging the Canadian people to be understanding and to make every effort to save the Canadian economy, to stop the boom before there was a bust. The people were asked to tighten their
Bank Act
belts in order to cut down the cost of living. The minister came in with taxes here and taxes there. We now have the bank bill before the committee, and what is the minister doing to reduce the cost of living? He is permitting the banks to increase the interest rate which will increase the cost of production in this country. It will affect everything. The minister does not speak, he just bows his head. One can only judge that the master has spoken and the servant has listened. If the minister wants to be a servant, then certainly I do not want to be a servant, and for this reason I will support the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage in the consideration of Bill No. C-222, we still have something to say. We have an amendment to move on the interest rate.
A while ago we had the pleasure of voting with the Conservatives to maintain the interest rate at 6 per cent. Unfortunately, I think some Conservatives who are in cahoots with big finance went into hiding and did not vote. That is why the amendment was defeated.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether there is some joking in this house or whether people are serious. Had the Conservatives been serious, they would certainly have voted on this important bill.
They want the people to believe they are working for them, that they are on their side, but they are against them. We on this side of the house, Mr. Chairman, are with the people and we can certify we are with them. Whenever we move an amendment, we are here to vote, even if we are few in number. We are not in such great number as the Conservative members, but our amendments are moved with conviction and by true representatives of the people.
As regards this clause 91, it is felt that the profit margin and the stock increase are not sufficient, with an interest rate, the ceiling of which is set at 6 per cent. Now, if we remove the ceiling and if the rate of interest goes up to 7-j, 8, 9 and even 10 per cent, and perhaps up to 12 per cent, or if there is no ceiling at all, the bank shares at a $10 par value will certainly go up to $100 and even more. Dividends will perhaps go up from $4 to $5 per share, which will represent a profit of 50 or 60 per cent on $10 shares.
Then, where will the ambition of the financiers end, since they are already enjoying an exclusive privilege belonging to the parliament of Canada, which represents the people, and not only to bank presidents and directors and to their shareholders?

Again, we would like to set the interest ceiling at more than 6 per cent on money created by means of guarantees from individual borrowers, companies, corporations, and federal, provincial and municipal governments.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring forward an amendment to clause 91. When it comes to allowing chartered banks to lend banking credits at more than 6 per cent, do we not feel that this is going to result in a federal increase in the rate of interest? We asked all the financiers, all the bankers who appeared before the committee whether they did not feel the increase in the rate of interest would result in an increase in the cost of living and they answered: No. They also answered that more money had to be put into circulation, that it would be easier for the small industrialists or for the small wage-earners to have more money.
Therefore Mr. Chairman, when one knows that Canadian citizens are up to their ears in debt at present, when one knows that they can hardly borrow, that the credit of three quarters of the people is not good any more, because they are far too indebted, in brief when one knows that the majority of the people do not want to borrow any more, since they are sure that they will not be able to repay, such are the conditions our friends opposite are creating. With every means at their disposal, they protect high finance and high society at the expense of the people. They are working against the people and the people will become aware of it one fine day.

This is the banks' main argument: they are asking for the removal of the 6 per cent ceiling on the interest rate so as to be able to compete with other financial institutions not subject to the same ceiling. Would it not be advisable, Mr. Chairman, to also set a ceiling for the other financial institutions, thus preventing at the same time an increase in the cost of living, in production costs and the rise of the whole economy?
The Minister of Finance resorts to this argument. He says it would be unfair to freeze the interest rate at 6 per cent if other institutions have the advantage of lending their money at higher rates. To my mind, that is not a valid argument. The duty and the responsibility of this parliament was to set a ceiling and to put all institutions on the same footing. That is what we should have done, but we did not do it. We did not face up to our responsibilities.
March 21, 1967

Gentlemen opposite, you have voted against your responsibilities. You have overlooked your responsibilities to the people in order once again to protect high finance, which already has everything, controls everything and exploits everything, and nobody can even breathe without its consent. You have forgotten that, hon. members opposite.
It is a known fact that the cost of an issue now totals from 10 to 20 per cent: the advertising, the sale, the printing. The capital is issued as new money and entered into the books of the chartered banks purchasing such bonds and the interest is paid out of taxes on the people and it is the system of eternal interest, debts and capital created by a stroke of the pen.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it is the responsibility of the state to differentiate between the two economic sectors-the private and the public sectors. And the major role is played particularly in the public sector. It is mostly in the public sector that the banks have the advantage of using their pen to create money. It is in the public sector that the various bonds of public bodies, the federal government as well as all other governments, provincial, municipal, school and parishes, are issued and it is through such bonds that the large financial institutions create credit and multiply credit with the ink in their pens.
That, Mr. Chairman, is fictitious money. That is money which should not be created by the financiers. That should be the responsibility of the Bank of Canada. In fact, it was the responsibility of our friends opposite and their Conservative neighbours to vote a moment ago to maintain the interest rate at 6 per cent. I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) went hiding because he is in collusion with high finance.
Mr. Chairman, we could still make important speeches. Take the case of the Cuban government. When they needed $2 billion to refinance their country's economy, they tried to secure money from the United States. They could not have it unless they were ready to pay 5, 5J and 6 per cent. So they asked Russia and that country is now financing the Cuban government at an interest rate of 1 per cent. If the communists are able to finance different nations at a rate of 1 per cent, Canadians should be able to finance their institutions at a reasonable rate of interest and not at 7, 8, 10 or 15 per cent, in other words, at all sorts of rates.
Bank Act
e (10:40 p.m.)
It is unfair to the people to refuse to fix a 6 per cent ceiling on the interest rate. I think this is the greatest injustice ever witnessed by parliament, and it will have serious consequences.
Today, the people are beginning to know, to understand, in other words, to read between the lines. There are people who have known extreme poverty, who have been sabotaged by high finance, and who remember it, who remember the interest rate they had to pay and how they lost their property.
A great number of citizens are going bankrupt right now, because the present system is taking away from them their property, all they possess, is taking away from them the work of several generations. In fact the present system does not hold water, since it cannot operate otherwise than by elevating a group of citizens and bringing down another one.
There is another group that has to go bankrupt, because it has to reimburse money created with nothing and on which interest is required. In fact, they require the repayment of capital created with pen and ink; they require money from the Bank of Canada, they require actual money in return.
The present system does not hold water, and this is why we see bankruptcies of all kinds, people who are turned out on the street, on the road, people who lose all they have.
This is what the gentlemen opposite voted for. It is the situation with which we are familiar at the present time.
And there is talk of changing this situation. You would not change it for all the tea in China because of your ties with big business. I think a certain number of people among you are bank shareholders living off the interest paid on their capital. And that is why you do not want to change this situation. But tomorrow morning the people will ask that it be changed.
Why, Mr. Chairman, is dissatisfaction rife in Canada nowadays? Why are unions mushrooming out in every sectors? To try and organize structures to help their members make a living. These structures could have been established by the governments, but they did not assume their responsibilities, they did not set up the structures, and these unions have to unite, to organize and come before the government, and face the people who have these responsibilities and who did not want to assume them.

March 21, 1967
Bank Act
You have seen that happen today with the Farmers' Union. They came over here; they are all on the verge of bankruptcy. They are deeply in debt. Therefore, to help them out, lend them money at a higher rate of interest. Mr. Chairman, it is like throwing a drowning man an anchor to submerge him further instead of throwing him a life-saving jacket.
The people are being submerged further into debt by all kinds of financial schemes, by raising interest rates thereby increasing the over-all cost of living and depreciating the purchasing power of our currency in foreign countries, in all the countries of the world, thus placing Canada in an unfavourable position.
This financial system of ours does not hold water; it works in favour of a few financiers to the detriment of 99 per cent of the people, perhaps more.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, many reforms should be made, but the government failed to introduce them. As far as we are concerned, we moved many amendments, but you have voted them down. They would have opened the way to do so many things for the people; we could have helped the citizens to have a more decent living, to benefit from the present system, to take advantage of scientific progress, to get an education and improve themselves from all points of view. Alas, we cannot even develop our natural resources.
Our present financiers do not even bother to develop our natural resources, and we are forced to let our Canadian fellow countrymen beg on their knees for the Americans to come in and develop our public and private wealth, our natural resources, because we have no money. The federal, provincial, municipal governments as well as the school boards endeavour to tap the people's savings, but there is not a single cent left in our society.
When one wishes to create or expand industries, develop our natural resources, well, there is no more capital, because it has all been absorbed by the present system to pay interest to financiers, to pay interest on money that does not exist, on fictitious money.
This is our situation, Mr. Chairman. These are the fields where great improvements would be necessary. And you were not willing to assume your responsibilities, you, members opposite, and you, Conservatives, and even you, New Democrats. In fact, you voted against almost every amendment we moved and which would have meant so much for the people. You all protect high finance.
[Mr. Latulippe.l
I therefore move an amendment to maintain at 6 per cent the interest on private loans, and at 2 per cent, the rate on public loans, because government bonds do not cost anything to those gentlemen, the financiers. Citizens have to make sacrifices to pay interest, to maintain the present system which is so bad for society, for the citizens, for the families, and which prevents the development of Canada in every respect. Now, you should vote for this amendment because you refused to allow the Bank of Canada to take over the control of money and credit, to create the credit required to finance public undertakings. We ask financiers to take their responsibilities. We ask the government that the financiers be forced to deprive themselves a little and loan that money at cost. It is claimed that costs amount to a little over 1 per cent.
That is why we have set at 2 per cent the rate on the money which will be created to finance the provinces, the municipalities and the public bodies.
Mr. Chairman, I would very much like to see those who were elected to represent the citizens really and properly, assume their responsibilities so that every Canadian might live decently.
I know quite well this amendment will be defeated. On the other hand, I shall have had the satisfaction of moving it. I shall have had the satisfaction of saying that I work for those who elected me, for the people and not only for the financial interests. I am not against high finance: I even want to give it the right to live. But I also want it to allow the citizens to live.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words about this amendment. The hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) suggests that while maintaining the interest rate at 6 per cent, on the loans made to a public body-namely the federal and provincial governments, municipalities and school boards-the banks should have a 2 per cent interest.
And this is justifiable, Mr. Chairman, since our present system, as the hon. Minister of Finance admitted according to my previous reference, the new money lent by the banks is simply created money. Since banks do not have to pay any interest on it, but draw some, they can lend this money at the rate of 2 per cent to the governments and still make a profit of 2 per cent.
If the amendment were carried, the banks could lend the money they have on deposit, at the rate of 6 per cent, and that portion of money they create, which represents the yearly advance of the Canadian economy, could be loaned at 2 per cent to the government only.
Mr. Chairman, was any thought given to all the savings that could thus be made in municipal, provincial and, indeed, federal budgets? For instance, when you think of the fact the federal government alone pays $1,280 million a year in interest, you can easily imagine what kind of savings it would make if it could get a 2 per cent interest rate, that is three times less than what it now pays. In
Bank Act
fact, instead of paying $1,280 million interest per year, it would pay only $400 million, which would mean additional available funds of some $800 million each year. Those additional funds could be used for many more useful things than what it is now used for.
In this way, the government, for instance, could give back to the provinces part of the tax revenue, to enable them to develop the field of education. Such amounts could be spent on public works which would allow the hiring of the unemployed we now have. They could also be used to increase family allowances and old age security pensions. When you think of what $800 million per year means, you realize that it is an amount which could be of tremendous usefulness to the Canadian people, as the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe) said a while ago. I think that measure would be a compromise between those who support the present system and those who advocate a new system of debt-free money. At least with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac, it would only be a reform of the present system and at that time, instead of interest-free loans by the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks would again continue to make loans and get an interest of 2 per cent-instead of not getting any at all-only when it comes to loans to public bodies.
If you stop to consider the savings it would mean for the federal, provincial and municipal governments, it would represent money available to the Canadian citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I want to support that amendment because I am convinced that if the house approves it the chartered banks might not benefit from it-although that will not make them poorer-but rather the 20 million Canadians.
The house can choose between the chartered banks and 20 million Canadians. By its vote, the house will indicate if it prefers to serve the chartered banks or 20 million Canadians.
Personally, Mr. Chairman, I will vote for the amendment because I prefer to vote for the interest and the welfare of 20 million Canadians rather than for the chartered banks.

Shall we wait, here, in Canada, until we have communism, when the banks shall be under state control as they are in Russia where all banks are now state property? Is it not possible, in a private enterprise regime to have an adequate financial system that would make it possible to finance the public sector at a lower interest rate than that we are now paying; in short, at an interest rate that would allow the country, the provinces, the municipalities and the school boards to finance themselves more easily?
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that the government can bring the Canadian banks to their senses, and if they are reasonable enough, they should look around them and across the Iron Curtain. They will suffer tomorrow the consequences of their present attitude; if not in five years, then in ten years. If this ends in bloody revolution, the banks, the "controllers" of the economic blood of the nation will be responsible for it.
Mr. Chairman, it is time to take the necessary steps to have the Canadian public protected and respected. Clause 1, Mr. Chairman, deals with the title of the act. I suggest that the title ought to be "the fluctuating interest rates act-an act to abdicate the government's responsibility for monetary policy".
Fluctuating interest rates are not conducive to stability and the orderly development of this nation, its industrial and economic life. This measure introduces a new factor of instability into monetary policy. It robs the Minister of Finance of some of the powers he now has to control monetary policy and it surrenders to the banks part of the responsibility that should and must remain in the hands of the government, through the Minister of Finance.
Interest rates can now work at cross purposes with those of monetary policy. This is not a good nor a worthwhile development. In my opinion it cannot have any but undesirable effects; in extreme circumstances such a policy could have disastrous effects.

speechtext:
Some of the people who are complaining most vehemently against the seal fishery would think nothing of using a rod and line to hook a salmon and play the poor unfortunate fish for hours just for sport. The practice of catching the salmon or trout on a line and playing it for an extended period of time before finally bringing it to shore to allow it to gasp itself to death is accepted, as
March 21, 19G7	COMMONS DEBATES	14319
it should be; and it certainly cannot be compared to the quick, merciful killing of a seal. It is unfortunate that animals must die to sustain life, but it is necessary in order that man can have food and clothing and that he can feed and educate his children.
I returned just last week from a brief visit to my riding where I reviewed the sealing practices with many of my constituents, all of whom ask only for the right to work for a living and the right to use the best possible tools to do the job. I can assure this house that there is no cruelty in the seal hunt. Seals are killed either by a sudden blow or by a quick shot, and are killed instantaneously-faster by far than the death of some of our domestic animals.
The Department of Fisheries and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) have done excellent work in bringing in regulations and in getting agreements from other countries to control the size of the herds, and the need for regulation is recognized. If the herds were allowed to become too large the effect on the commercial fishery would be disastrous. The amount of bait fishes, of salmon and of shell fishes that would be consumed by these animals would deplete the supply to a tremendous extent. It should be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that even today it is necessary in some cases to provide a bounty on certain seals in order to protect certain of the fishes. The same people who now complain about the killing of seals would soon complain if the number of salmon and other game fish in our rivers were reduced by the appetites of an excessive seal population.
It would be impossible, Mr. Speaker, to speak about sealing without thinking of the gaff, the traditional tool of the sealer which has saved many a sealer's life on treacherous icefields both in preventing him from falling into the water and in assisting him in recovering on an occasion when he might fall in. Because of the importance of the hunt for those taking seals from the shore, it is imperative that the use of shotguns and shells be continued, as expensive rifles are not available to everyone and slugs are not as effective as shot. The thought of high powered rifles being fired from small boats on a misty morning is one that brings visions of possible tragic results, and is something that is not necessary. The fisherman taking seals from the shore must be allowed to use the equipment that is best suited for the task at hand. He must be able to use the best boats that he has for the job and the boats to which he is accustomed.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that the Department of Fisheries is very much interested in the welfare and in the well being of the fishermen on the eastern coast of Canada, as well as the western coast of Canada. However, the Department of Fisheries has taken steps in the past, and will continue to do so, to ensure that this fishery is carried out in as humane a way as possible. While it is unfortunate that certain unfounded publicity from time to time has been spread about regarding certain aspects of the seal fishery, there is also ample evidence to suggest the killing of seals is carried out in a way which, in many instances, is more humane than that carried out in the killing of other animals.
I might say that personally, like the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, I sometimes find it a little inconsistent to hear big game hunters and big game fishermen advocate the abolition of the seal fishery while they find it easy to spend an hour or an hour and a half playing a fish on a line. I think it may be helpful to some people if there were a clear distinction between the two forms of killing. Perhaps some would even suggest the seal fishery was not as cruel, if that is the right way of putting it, as sport fishing.
In conclusion, I can assure the hon. member the Department of Fisheries has and will continue to have a great interest in fishermen in all types of fishery and at the same time will hope to see to it that as fair and as humane regulations as possible are introduced in this aspect of the fishery, as in all other aspects.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-RESEAECH INTO ILLNESS CAUSED BY NOISE
speechtext:
Living, as I normally do, in relative solitude, I notice the city noise in all its amplitude and it is tor that reason I have taken a particular interest in the damaging effect of the noise of modern society. This is important to communities, to working people generally and to the general public. It is for that reason I have been interested in the subject. I have read the report on noise published by the World Health Organization, and its effect as a public nuisance as shown in studies of occupational research. I have also read the final report presented to parliament by the lord president of the council and minister for science, by command of Her Majesty, July 1963, in the parliament of Great Britain, which deals with this question in a very interesting way and makes some recommendations.
[DOT] (12:30 a.m.)
My attention was directed to this subject the other day on account of an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 15, 1967 entitled: "Sue over noise, workers urged". It reads as follows:
Thousands of persons working in British factories may be in a position to claim compensation for damage to their hearing caused by noise.
J. B. Cronin of the Southampton University law faculty told a scientific meeting at the Royal Society in London that employees could successfully claim for bodily injury caused by employers' negligence. Yet no employee had ever taken such action.
"I don't know what the trade unions have been at," Mr. Cronin said.
Professor E. J. Richards, of Southampton University's institute of sound and vibration research, told the meeting that there was already ample evidence that many a worker's hearing was being permanently damaged by noisy working conditions-and as the power and size of machinery increased, the noise problem would get worse.
Mr. Speaker, the general effect of noise is, in the first instance, on the physical health of the body. For the most part people's well being is diminished by noise. In this sense of the term there is no doubt that noise affects health. It has been proven to affect the mental health of some people and to affect the
DEBATES	March 21, 1967
enjoyment of communication based on sound in relation to hearing. It can affect working efficiency, and also the incidence of industrial accidents. I have had some personal experience in connection with the operation of mine compressors and machines of that sort-not that I have worked in the place, but I was an observer. In my opinion noise is an occupational hazard and a public nuisance in modern society. Research is required in an effort to provide remedies and compensation for those who suffer from noise in industry and in other segments of our communities.
It was for that reason that on Wednesday, March 15, I asked the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare whether any research is being undertaken in Canada at the present time in damage done to the human body as the result of noise.
The fair lady listens with dignity and poise,
To my inquiries about research and noise,
I hope her reply will be complete and good Based on homework well done, as it should.

Mr. Speaker, the answer to the hon. member's question is yes, the government is concerned about the effects of noise, both on the human body and on the mind. For example, over the past several years research assistance from the public health research grant has been given to a number of studies on the relation of noise to hearing loss. I understand that the Medical Research Council and the Defence Research Board have also given grants for research in this area. In addition, we do know of various university activities in this field. We would be pleased to have a list of these research activities prepared for the hon. member for Kootenay West, if he so desires.
Mr. Speaker, if I may end this very brief reply on the same note as that of the hon. member for Kootenay West, I would say that: The hon. member for Kootenay West Asks lots of questions, as do the rest.
